events.title: The ghost cartel — your pricing algorithm may have stopped competing without your knowledge
events.summary: In its antitrust suit against Amazon , the Federal Trade Commission described a pricing tool internally named Project Nessie. The system identified products where competitors were likely to follow an Amazon price increase, raised the price, and held it once rivals matched. The agency alleges the tool generated more than $1 billion in excess profit — and that Amazon paused it during periods of heightened scrutiny, then switched it back on. Amazon disputes this and says the tool was discontinued years ago. That is the deliberate version of this problem: a company designing a system to anticipate rivals. The harder version is the one nobody designs at all. In 2017, when automated pricing software became widely available to German gas stations, economists later found that in markets where two competing stations both adopted it, margins rose by about 38% — with no meeting, no message, and no agreement between them. Market-level margins didn’t move at all when only one station in a market adopted the software. The rise appeared only when two algorithms were left to set prices, in effect, against each other, a pattern consistent with each one learning on its own that it earned more by backing off. That study, published in the Journal of Political Economy in 2024 , is among the first real-world measurements of a problem previously shown mostly in simulation. Pricing algorithms can produce the economic outcome of a cartel, meaning higher prices sustained over time, without the conduct antitrust law was written to detect. It matters for any company that has handed pricing to software, because the behavior may not appear on the dashboards used to judge whether the software works. Executives usually judge competition by the pressure they feel, and a market where prices hold and margins stay comfortable reads as one they have won. Automated pricing breaks that instinct. When autonomous agents set prices, the same calm picture can mean the opposite, a sign that competition has quietly stopped because the algorithms have learned that leaving each other alone pays better than fighting. The failure that should concern leaders is subtle. An algorithm that sets an obviously wrong price is easy to catch. The harder case is one that does exactly what it was designed to do, optimize margin, and reaches an outcome the company would struggle to justify in public. Three ways competition quietly disappears Competition can fade in more than one way. Independently deployed algorithms, each pursuing its own profit, can learn over repeated encounters to stop undercutting one another, with no one designing the outcome and no data changing hands. Call it the ghost: no agreement, no data exchange, no one who designed it — just two systems that arrived at the same truce independently. A single firm can instead use software to anticipate how rivals will react, raising a price where it predicts they will follow, a unilateral strategy rather than a pact. Call it the mirror: Amazon’s Nessie belongs here — no pact, just a system built to predict a rival’s reflection and act first. Or competitors feed their data into a common provider whose algorithm guides them all, the pattern enforcers find easiest to challenge. Call it the hub: RealPage is the textbook case , and it’s the only one of the three regulators have actually managed to touch. The first is this article’s subject, the hardest to see and hardest for the law to reach. The clearest evidence comes from controlled experiments. In a paper published in the American Economic Review in 2020 , four economists set reinforcement-learning algorithms to compete in a standard model of repeated pricing. The algorithms could not communicate and were told only to maximize profit. They consistently learned to charge above the competitive level, and to enforce it. When one lowered its price to gain share, the others cut theirs, then returned to the higher level once it fell back into line. The pattern held even when firms differed in cost or demand and when the number of competitors changed. The four authors, joined by Wharton economist Joseph Harrington, set out the policy stakes in Science later that year . They warned that delegating pricing to algorithms opens a backdoor to collusion, since AI can learn collusive rules with no human oversight or awareness. Harrington has argued that competition law must be rethought for coordination that arises without agreement. The German gasoline data indicates that this happens in practice and not only in a model. Not every experiment reaches the same conclusion, though, and researchers still debate how readily these results carry over to live markets. That uncertainty is itself a reason for boards to watch behavior now, rather than wait for regulators to settle the question for them. Why the law struggles with this Antitrust enforcement was designed around human agreement, evidence of a meeting or understanding between competitors. Coordination a machine learns on its own provides none of that, which is why even the most prominent recent case, built around a shared vendor, proved so hard to resolve. In 2024, the Department of Justice and several states sued RealPage, whose software recommended rents using data from competing properties, along with landlords that used it. In November 2025 the DOJ filed a proposed settlement . RealPage paid no penalty and admitted no wrongdoing. The terms mainly restrict the data the software may draw on — barring recent competitor data and the fine-grained local geography that made neighborhood-level coordination possible — and install a court-appointed monitor. The settlement still needs court approval, and the wider litigation continues. RealPage is the easier case, a common provider pooling competitors’ nonpublic data into one recommendation. The harder case begins when independently deployed systems reach the same result using nothing but the prices they can all observe. There is no hub to point to, and nothing that resembles a meeting. Two recent appellate rulings, both involving the same vendor’s software, drew this line for us. The Ninth Circuit dismissed a case against Las Vegas hotels because the tool did not pool their confidential data. A year later, the Third Circuit revived a near-identical case against Atlantic City casinos, where competitors did feed nonpublic data into the shared system and followed its output about nine times in ten. Pooled competitor data on one side and independent use of the same tool on the other is the boundary between RealPage and the harder case. Legislators have not waited, either. Starting with San Francisco in the summer of 2024, cities including Philadelphia , Minneapolis and Seattle banned algorithmic rent-setting tools. events.title: I let my 15-year-old fly home alone from Europe. It didn't go smoothly, but I'm still glad she earned the independence.
events.summary: The author (right) allowed her teenage daughter to fly home from Spain by herself. Courtesy of Jamie Davis Smith When I booked an extended-family trip to Europe, my teenage daughter complained it was too long. I agreed to let her fly home early by herself, even though I was nervous and reluctant. She forgot her passport and faced delays, but she got home safely. Most summers, I try to pack in as much travel as possible with my kids. My children have dual citizenship , and it's important to me that they spend time in Europe and connect with their roots. I enjoy showing them the rest of the world, too. In past years, my kids have had fun traveling from Rome to Warsaw or Seoul to Tokyo. This summer, I planned on staying in Europe for nearly a month, making the most of our time by staying until the day before school started. I booked hotels and flights and excitedly told my kids the plan. But this year went a bit differently than expected. I allowed my teenage daughter to travel home alone. My daughter wasn't happy when she heard about my extended travel plans When my 11-year-old son learned we would be spending nearly a month in Europe, he was overjoyed. My 15-year-old daughter, however, was despondent. She wanted to spend time with her friends. Plus, she worried about meeting her school obligations , which include a leadership position in a school club and cross-country and track training. She begged me to cut the trip short. However, I wasn't willing to end my trip early. I had hard-to-get tickets to a Real Madrid soccer match for the last day of the trip. My son and I are both huge soccer fans , and I didn't want to miss the game. Desperate, my daughter started listing the meetings and practices she would miss if we stayed in Europe until just before school began. My daughter asked if she could fly home alone Unwilling to accept no for an answer, my daughter sprang into action. She didn't whine and complain. Instead, she researched whether she could fly home alone and presented me with the facts. She showed me that I could change her flight, booked with points, at no extra cost. She presented airline policies indicating that she was old enough to fly alone without paying an unaccompanied minor fee, and that there were no restrictions on American minors flying alone from Spain to the US. She also found a direct flight from Madrid to Washington, DC , which greatly reduced the chances of something going wrong. My daughter made a convincing case, and I reluctantly agreed. I tried to think of everything that could go wrong. I signed a letter giving her permission to travel solo and had it notarized. I made sure she had a phone, credit card, and cash in case she needed it. Nevertheless, I was still reluctant and didn't fully commit to the plan until the night before her flight. I told my daughter that I wanted her to stay, but if she left early, she was responsible for packing, getting up on time, and making sure she had everything she needed. Even with preparation, things didn't go entirely smoothly Although I wasn't fully behind my daughter's plans to leave our family vacation early, I told her I would accompany her to the airport in case she ran into any problems or changed her mind. Despite all of my planning, things didn't go entirely smoothly. I had suggested leaving our hotel well before flight departure time in case she ran into any issues leaving the country as a solo 15-year-old traveler. She disagreed with my timeframe, preferring to get a little more sleep and enjoy the hotel's buffet. I was a little concerned, but I deferred to her judgment. When she was ready, we hopped into a taxi. However, halfway to the airport, my daughter realized she had forgotten her passport at the hotel. I explained the situation to our driver in broken Spanish , and he drove like a madman to rush us back. When we arrived at the airport, frazzled and rushed, I had to quickly kiss my daughter on the cheek and wish her a good flight. I waited until she texted me that she was through before heading back into the city, even though a piece of my heart was about to fly across the Atlantic without me. I expected to hear from my daughter next when she landed. However, I received regular updates over the next two hours. She was stuck on the tarmac because of the weather, bored and unsure whether her flight would ever take off. "You can always come back to the hotel," I reminded her, but she ignored me. Her flight finally took off, but midway through, the passenger next to her stepped on her headphones, so she couldn't watch movies or listen to music for the last half of her long journey across the ocean. But she made it home safely My daughter enjoyed the rest of her summer the way she wanted to. I'm glad I let her take this huge leap toward independence. Although it's sometimes hard for me to accept that my little girl is growing up, I knew she was ready to decide when it was time to leave and travel halfway across the world on her own. Leaving her at the airport was just one of many goodbyes I know are coming as she gets older and creates her own life. I'm glad I gave her the opportunity to prove that she is ready. events.title: Moving from New York to Kentucky gave me an affordable life I love — and retiring at 55 is now on the table
events.summary: Nick Lyktey went to Kentucky to fulfill a one-year working requirement, and stayed years later. Courtesy of Nick Lyktey New Yorker Nick Lyktey moved to Kentucky for work, thinking he'd only be there for one year. He ended up falling in love with Fort Wright, Kentucky, a suburb five miles outside Cincinnati. He says the state's relative affordability has helped him build a better financial future for his family. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Nick Lyktey, 34, a New Yorker who grew up in Wantagh, on Long Island, but moved to Fort Wright, Kentucky, five miles outside Cincinnati. He now works as the chief of lab operations at Gravity Diagnostics and has lived in Kentucky for seven years. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I had a very set trajectory ever since the eighth grade; I knew what I wanted to do with my life. Every move I made was based on working for the FBI . I went to Penn State specifically because they have a really elite forensic science program where they have buildings on campus dedicated for crime scene analysis. Even going to graduate school at Indiana University, that eliminated needing a larger amount of job experience required to get into the FBI . After graduate school, I talked to a contact at the FBI and they said, "With your master's, you just need one year of work experience before you can be accepted into the special agent program." I'd always envisioned myself living on the East Coast . I liked growing up on Long Island. I didn't necessarily think I'd return to Long Island , but I wanted to be on the coast, and I think my familiarity with the East Coast would allow me to pick that over the West Coast. I was applying to a bunch of jobs eastward of Indiana, and I didn't hate the idea of being out this way. I felt like I had friends in different areas of the country, and the cost of living was great. I had a lot of good opportunities, and I narrowed down my job search to two companies, both in Kentucky. Lyktey at the Newport Aquarium with his wife and parents. Courtesy of Nick Lyktey When I went to visit the locations, I felt like this is somewhere I could live. My mindset was, "I'm just going to be here for a year," so even if I'm not in love with the area right now, it's only a year, because ultimately I'm going to go to Quantico and go to bootcamp and then get placed somewhere else." My area of Kentucky is more suburban and less rural than I expected I didn't think Kentucky was going to be as urban or suburban as it ended up being. I thought it was going to be a little bit more rural, with maybe not as much access to things. When I was telling my family about the move, my mom, who was born and raised on Long Island, would always make jokes to me. She would be like, "You're going to get a pickup truck," or "It's probably just a bunch of farms." I was like, "No, no, it's pretty built up." My expectations were that Fort Wright was going to be a smaller, less populated city; if I live in Kentucky, I'm going to go to Cincinnati all the time. That was the energy I had, but I was looking at it as more of a short-term scope. After I moved in, when my mom visited me, she would always say, "This is a little paradise." Lyktey with his mother and wife at a Cincinnati Reds game. Courtesy of Nick Lyktey I live in a really nice little suburb. It's a great community where people are taking your garbage can in for you if you come home late from work. I think that's something that was similar to Long Island. I grew up in the suburb of all suburbs, and it was similar in the sense of community — houses along the street together — but in Kentucky, you have a little more space than you would in New York. There's also a lot of growth and development in this region, and I want to be somewhere that's better every single year. I feel like this area is doing that. I miss my family and friends all the time, but it's a good community here. The life I have with my wife here is phenomenal. We're in a good, comfortable place and we're happy with where we are. We're happy with our jobs and happy with the environment surrounding us. Kentucky gave me the financial flexibility I never thought I'd have I never talked about the word " retirement " in my life. I don't see myself as being a good retiree . I thought I'd be working until I'm in the grave. I didn't think I'd be able to take vacation. I thought I'd be monitoring my budget really frequently. With the amount of money we're saving by living in Kentucky , we're able to do renovations on the house , and we're able to take vacations freely. I'm not as anally retentive about our budget as I thought we were going to be. We've had conversations with our financial advisor, and he's like, "This is a reasonable plan for you to retire at 55 ." My mom unfortunately passed away at 59, and I've been thinking about different things in life and the way they hit you — it completely changes your thinking. Both my parents had good jobs. They worked extremely hard. I knew they did well for themselves, but that was just to keep us all afloat. Now, it's a luxury to be able to go on vacations or be able to get the best things for my daughter. That matters the most to me in the world. Having that financial flexibility is really powerful. I have a bunch of friends who we're all in the same stage of life together. A lot of them still live on Long Island and they're buying houses and having kids. We talk about these financial things and I realized we live in radically different worlds.My wife and I were able to get a pretty nice starter family home with a fenced-in backyard. We have two dogs and we have one daughter, and I think it's a comfortable way of living where our mortgage isn't suffocating. Lyktey in front of his home with his wife and his daughter. Courtesy of Nick Lyktey One of my buddies on Long Island bought a house that was listed at $650,000 and they closed at $750,000 — and it's a fixer-upper. Our house was $230,000, and it was ready to go in a nice suburb close to work. I love where I grew up and I have no issues there, but we have a lot more financial flexibility and can do a lot more here. It's like a chemical shift in your brain because I never grew up in that type of environment, where you can afford this life. All of our friends, all of our family, everybody worked really hard and they were really great people doing the best they could for their family. But affording things always felt, to me, rather suffocating and stressful. Kentucky has provided me with a life that I didn't even think was a possibility, and I didn't even realize it was within grasp. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The world reconsiders America
events.summary: America is shedding its status as the default choice for foreign governments to park money, buy weapons and send students. Why it matters: Even modest shifts away from the U.S. could chip away at advantages that have helped sustain American economic and geopolitical power for decades. Driving the news: The Netherlands moved 86 tons of gold out of the U.S. and Canada last week, citing the move as a hedge against "extreme systemic risks." France already moved all of its gold out of New York, while Germany debated doing the same. Norway's sovereign wealth fund — the world's largest — announced plans to reduce its holdings of U.S. government bonds amid turbulence in the Treasury market. The big picture: Beyond finance, European countries are looking for ways to wean off the U.S. On weapons, Europe is seeking to source more equipment locally to reduce its dependence on American firepower, Reuters reports. On technology, the EU this summer set out plans to reduce its reliance on American companies, drafting cloud rules that would restrict Amazon, Google and Microsoft from competing for sensitive contracts, Reuters also reported . Zoom out: Individuals around the world are also recalibrating their relationship to the U.S. International applications to U.S. colleges dropped 10% in the most recent admissions cycle. Stricter international student visa policies and the Trump administration's broader immigration posture have weighed heavily. International travel to the U.S. fell 5.5% in 2025, the first decline since the pandemic, as relationships with longtime allies grew strained. Canadian travel dropped 25% last year, with the slide continuing into early 2026. German travel to the U.S. has dropped 25% since the beginning of Trump's term, with the country's travel association pointing to politics as one factor. By the numbers: America's standing has been hit especially hard in the West, according to a recent Pew study . Hungary and Poland were the only two of 10 countries polled where majorities still view the U.S. as a reliable partner. Majorities in all 10, including two with right-wing populist leaders, say they lack confidence in Trump to do the right thing in world affairs. Reality check: This is not wholesale abandonment of U.S. partnership. The U.S. dollar's dominance remains unthreatened, allies depend heavily on American military might and the U.S. remains the top destination for international students. What to watch: Germany, Italy and Spain are facing renewed pushes at home over whether to keep gold reserves in the U.S.

events.title: Dell's 52-inch enormo-monitor is a tsunami of impractical fun
events.summary: FIRST LOOK Dell's UltraSharp 52 display is a joyously enormous head-turner, but probably too much monitor for most users. Dell debuted the display at the CES show earlier this year. It's now on sale for $3,000. Sadly, I lack a PC capable of driving the screen at its full 6144 x 2560 resolution and 120 Hz refresh rate. Even at a miserly 3840 x 2160, however, I often marveled at how much it could display. Consider the screenshot below, which shows 50 columns and 89 rows of a single Excel spreadsheet – 4,450 cells in total. Here's another look at the monitor in full flight: a screen grab of Zwift, the virtual cycling metaverse I visit regularly as part of my exercise routine. At that size, Zwift felt more immersive and enjoyable than it does on a smaller screen. The display also handled motion smoothly during Zwift. other games, and streamed video. Getting used to it It took me a while to appreciate the monitor. When I first plugged it in, my occasionally-stiff middle-aged neck strained as I swiveled to view content at the edges and corners, while wielding my mouse to move its pointer between the screen's extremities felt like flapping my arms. My eyes didn't enjoy the experience at first either. I wear mild reading glasses while working, and found myself repeatedly refocusing as I looked across the curved display. For the first few days I spent with the screen, I therefore practiced "pillarboxing" – running the display at 3840 x 2160 and only using the center of the monitor while pixels on the edges remained dark. That didn't feel odd or distracting, perhaps because I often use "letterboxing" while watching video on my TV or tablet – leaving pixels at the top and bottom of the screen unused. As I grew accustomed to the enormo-monitor, I began using its entire area. Getting there was not straightforward: each of the three PCs I used with the monitor (one at a time, not together) required manual adjustment before I found a resolution that did not distort text and images. Dell's companion app was no help. It was slow to install, ran as if stuck in digital treacle, and is little more than a glorified front end for the Windows System/Display control panel. The HDMI connection to my desktop – an Acemagic mini-PC – repeatedly dropped out, forcing me to reseat the cable every day. The same PC and cable work reliably with my everyday monitor. I tried another cable and the problem persisted. I reached out to Dell, who suggested my two different cables were to blame. I connected my laptop – a Dell Inspiron Plus 7441 – over Thunderbolt and experienced some flickering that went away without needing to reseat the cable. A ten-year-old ThinkPad Carbon X1 connected fine over HDMI, but had even more trouble finding appropriate settings. But once I got the machine going and got used to its colossal size, my initial fatigue vanished. I realized I was squinting a little less than I do with my everyday display, a seven-year-old 32-inch Samsung that lacks the HDR feature the Dell machine includes. I sometimes use my lunch breaks to watch some rugby highlights, and the display handled those with ease. The easily observable nuances of small ads on team shirts would doubtless please sponsors. I was also pleasantly surprised by the display's speakers, which rendered my favorite tunes brightly and crisply. My current high rotation tunes include guitar feedback legends The Jesus and Mary Chain, spiky garage pop from Welsh outfit The Bug Club, and mumbly "power disco" by Getdown Services. JAMC's trademark fuzz was warm and deep, I felt like I could hear new strings on The Bug Club's guitars, and Getdown Services' beats thumped meatily. The speakers' location at the rear of the monitor led to a few "Where's that sound coming from?" moments, but those quickly became tolerable. Weighty issues I was impressed by Dell's packaging, which places the cables and included stand in clearly marked cardboard compartments within the shell protecting the screen. That matters because the box is a whopper that would be difficult to lug out of an IKEA and into a small car. Easy access to the assembly parts means a little less wrestling. At 12.95 kg (28.5 lbs), the monitor isn't problematically heavy – but is maybe too weighty for Dell's stand, as it never sat perfectly level, and I could find no way to straighten it. The screen is also unwieldy: I recommend connecting any cables you plan to use in advance, because shifting and lifting it to access its ports is not easy, especially in constricted spaces behind a desk. Tucked under the monitor's bottom-left edge is a forward-facing USB hub with two USB-C ports and one USB-A port. Making one of them a Thunderbolt port would have made it easier to connect a laptop without rummaging behind the beast. I finished my time with this giant display convinced that it is a lovely machine, but not one I need, as my work consists mostly of writing and editing text and browsing the web. Those who work with visual material may adore its size and the immersion created by its gentle curve. Many of Dell's promotional images show the device displaying multiple financial data feeds. The company pitches it as a replacement for four smaller monitors, requiring only one power cable and dispensing with a complex collection of stands. That seems like a more sensible use of the screen than everyday knowledge work. To finish, here's one more photo. I started working from home in 2002 but had no room to dedicate to an office. I therefore splurged about $700 – big bucks at the time – on a 15-inch, 1024 x 768 Dell 1503FP LCD monitor so that a CRT did not dominate my lounge room. It still works, although when the time came to take this snap, I couldn't find the HDMI-to-VGA adapter I use to fire it up. Here it is anyway, posed in front of its giant descendant to offer some historical perspective on how monitors have grown. ®

events.title: Jewish institutions' security spending tops $1 billion as antisemitism persists
events.summary: Antisemitic threats have pushed the nationwide cost of protecting Jewish synagogues, schools and community centers past $1 billion a year, new estimates reveal as congregations prepare for big crowds during the High Holy Days , which began Friday with Rosh Hashanah. Why it matters: Enhanced security has become a growing expense for Jewish communities, congregation leaders say, often taking up money that could pay for teachers, summer camps, elder care and other programs. By the numbers: Jewish communal institutions are now spending an estimated $1.02 billion annually on security, a record high, according to new data from the Jewish Federations of North America (JFNA). That's up 33% from the federation's previous annual estimate of $765 million in 2024. More than 4,500 synagogues, Jewish community centers, schools, summer camps and other nonprofits spend an average of roughly $225,000 each, the group said. Security personnel — including guards and security directors — account for the largest share. Of that total, about $150 million goes toward security technology and the "hardening" of buildings — upgrades that can include security cameras, reinforced doors and controlled-entry systems — as well as maintaining existing security equipment. The estimate doesn't include security costs at more than 1,600 kosher restaurants, about 500 kosher markets and groceries, and other privately owned Jewish businesses. State of play: Synagogues are increasingly moving beyond security guards and cameras to layered, year-round systems that include hardened entrances , trained congregants as security personnel and coordination with police. More than 7,100 volunteers now help protect more than 500 synagogues and events each week, according to Community Security Service (CSS) , a nonprofit that now protects more than 500 synagogues across the U.S. The expanded security comes as assaults linked to antisemitism have reached their highest level since the Anti-Defamation League began tracking them in 1979. What they're saying: "I cannot tell you whether we're safer or less safe," CSS CEO Richard Priem told Axios. "I can tell you that there's a lot more capability right now protecting the Jewish community than there was a few years ago." JFNA CEO Eric Fingerhut said the tradeoff is stark. "Every dollar our community spends on guards and cameras is a dollar not spent on Jewish education." Context: The estimated Jewish communal security tab is more than three times the size of the entire federal grant pool available to vulnerable nonprofits nationwide. FEMA made $300 million available through the FY 2026 Nonprofit Security Grant Program for nonprofits at high risk of terrorist or extremist attacks. A bipartisan bill introduced in Congress this year, the Jewish American Security Act, would authorize $1 billion annually from FY 2027 through FY 2031 for the grant program, and loosen limits on using the money for security personnel. Yes, but: More recent data present a mixed picture. Antisemitic incidents surged after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, rising 140% that year and climbing again to a record high in 2024, according to the Anti-Defamation League . FBI data show reported anti-Jewish hate crime incidents fell 21% in 2025, from 1,938 to 1,528, but were still the third-most on record. Anti-Jewish incidents still accounted for about 63% of all religion-based hate crimes and 14% of all reported hate crimes last year. Separately, the ADL found overall antisemitic incidents fell 33% last year, even as physical assaults rose to a 46-year high.

events.title: My husband and I have a weekly marriage check-in. We use the same questions each time.
events.summary: A weekly check-in helps the couple talk about small annoyances before they snowball. Courtesy of Rebecca Strong My husband and I started having a weekly marriage meeting. It's helped us express gratitude for each other and prevented so many unnecessary arguments. This 30-minute weekly marriage ritual keeps small annoyances from turning into big fights. After having a baby last summer, my husband and I realized something: by the time the house was quiet and our baby was asleep, neither of us had much energy left to talk about anything. We weren't fighting often, but little frustrations had a way of lingering because there never seemed to be a "right" time to bring them up. So, we decided to try a new weekly check-in ritual . We treat it like a physical for our relationship: It's a chance to celebrate what's working, catch small issues before they snowball, and make sure neither of us is quietly carrying resentment. So far, it's been the single most helpful habit we've adopted as a couple. We use the same questions every week Having a structured format works well for us. Instead of wasting time — "What do you want to talk about?" "I don't know, what do you want to talk about?" — we just run down our list, each taking turns to talk or listen. While it took some trial-and-error to find the questions that are most beneficial, here's the set we landed on: What made you feel loved this week? What's your biggest stressor looking ahead to next week? And what's one thing I can do to support you? What's one thing you're really looking forward to this week? What would make you feel connected to me this week? Is there anything we should talk about now before it becomes a bigger issue? Each question serves a different purpose. Asking the same questions each week helps keep them on track. Courtesy of Rebecca Strong The first question encourages us to acknowledge each other's efforts During a busy, stressful week, it can be easy to overlook the little things we both do to care for each other. But my husband and I made a vow never to take each other for granted. The first question — "What made you feel loved this week?" — offers a natural opportunity for us to express some gratitude . I might let my husband know how much it meant to me that he got up with the baby in the middle of the night. He might thank me for making his morning easier by filling up his water bottle and watching our son while he worked out. Then, we do some collaborative troubleshooting I find that naming my stressors out loud can help prevent me from spiraling inside my own head. Plus, when my husband and I share them with each other, we're able to proactively problem-solve together. Better yet, we both have the chance to explain exactly how we'd like to receive support from each other — rather than leaving each other to guess. So, if I tell him I'm nervous about an interview coming up this week, he could offer some confidence-boosting affirmation, and then I could ask him to rehearse my questions with me the night before so I feel prepared. We also balance things out with positive anticipation During our check-in, we're careful not to dwell too much on the potentially anxiety-inducing events coming up. Taking a moment to talk about the things we're looking forward to, whether it's a family walk or a special home-cooked dinner , helps us to feel excited about the week ahead. We benefit from having an opportunity to express our needs My husband and I have similar love languages , but we're not mind readers. We can't expect the other person to know exactly what we need from each other. That's precisely why we started asking: "What would make you feel connected to me this week?" Sometimes, for me, it's often as simple as having breakfast together or getting a text check-in after my therapy appointment. For him, it might just be an unprompted hug or putting our phones away while we watch something together. They express their needs during their check-in. Courtesy of Rebecca Strong Finally, we tackle any issues before they escalate If there's one thing we've learned over the last eight years of our relationship, it's that there's a right and wrong time to bring up things that are bothering you. Confronting the other person at the end of a draining workday, or in a moment when one or both of you are already emotionally activated, is unlikely to lead to a productive discussion. That's why we always end our weekly check-ins on this question: Is there anything we should talk about now before it becomes a bigger issue? This gives us both peace of mind that there's a designated time to air out any concerns, so we don't feel the need to tackle them when we don't have the emotional bandwidth. In my iPhone Notes App, I might jot down something that bugged me — say, when my husband forgot to tell me he was working late — so I don't forget to bring it up. Sometimes, by the time we get to our weekly check-in on Sunday, I'm already over it. But when something is still bothering me, it's super helpful to have a safe space to share it. events.title: We know how to prevent black lung, so why are workers still dying?
events.summary: Silicosis sufferers are getting younger as Trump and the coal mining industry push back on protections Silicosis is one of the oldest workplace hazards and public health experts have known for decades how to prevent it. Yet a new wave of workers, from Appalachian coalminers to Latino countertop fabrication workers, are developing and dying from the disease as industry fights new protections and regulators fail to defend the rules that could protect them. John Robinson’s grandfather developed black lung back when coalminers could spend decades in the mines before being diagnosed with the disease, often dying in their 60s, 70s and 80s. But Robinson, who mined for coal in south-west Virginia, was diagnosed when he was 47. He’s part of a trend that has grown over the past two decades in central Appalachia, where more coalminers are developing black lung disease at younger ages. “Now, honey, how are these men getting sick? Something’s causing it,” Robinson said. “At one time, you didn’t say black lung around the coal site unless you wanted to lose a job. It’s such an outbreak right now they can’t hide it.” Around 2018, doctors throughout the US started documenting outbreaks of lung disease among countertop fabrication workers too. There were seven workers diagnosed in Colorado and another 12 cases in Texas. That same year, a 38-year-old Hispanic man in California, whose work involved grinding stone edges at a countertop fabrication company, died of respiratory failure. Public health experts say the cause of both outbreaks is inhalation of tiny crystalline silica dust on the job and prevention involves limiting workers’ exposure through sampling and tamping down the dust to stop particles from becoming airborne. This means different things depending on the occupation. For miners, the 2024 Mine Safety and Health Administration (Msha) rule years in the making and passed under the Biden administration was supposed to address the occupational hazard. But within months of the rule going into effect, industry groups petitioned to overturn it. When the Trump administration failed to defend the rule, the eighth circuit court of appeals stayed it and Msha notified the court that it will reconsider portions of the rule impacted by the industry challenge. The National Stone, Sand & Gravel Association (NSSGA) led the legal challenge of Msha’s 2024 silica dust rule. The trade group represents sand, gravel and stone mining companies. NSSGA did not oppose the rule’s reduction of the permissible exposure limit from 100 micrograms per cubic meter to 50 micrograms per cubic meter per eight-hour shift, said Kerry Lynch, NSSGA’s senior director of communications. Lynch did not respond to questions about why it brought the legal challenge of the rule. But in a letter to Msha before the rule was finalized, NSSGA said it takes issue with the frequent air sampling and medical surveillance requirements. The American Exploration & Mining Association (AEMA) is one of the industry groups that joined the petition to challenge Msha’s 2024 silica dust rule. In a written statement to the Guardian, AEMA’s executive director, Mark Compton said that the AEMA supports lowering the permissible exposure limit (PEL) of silica to better protect miners. “We joined the petition challenging the 2024 silica rule because the rule would actually undermine miner safety and health due to the restrictions Msha imposed on its implementation,” Compton said. “The rule takes an inflexible, cookie-cutter approach that doesn’t account for the variability in locations and types of actions at different operations, engineering controls are not always technically or economically feasible, contrary to Msha’s assertion in the 2024 rule. Greater use of administrative controls such as job rotation and acceptance of personal protective equipment in the form of respirators should be allowed to achieve and comply with the reduced PEL.” Countertop fabrication workers should be protected under a 2016 Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) rule , which also faced industry pushback when it was implemented. Industry groups including NSSGA challenged the rule in court, arguing that Osha’s stricter exposure limit was “not based on sound science”. The appeal to “sound science” has long been a tactic used by industries seeking to cast doubt on research that could lead to stricter regulation, a strategy that David Michaels, an epidemiologist and professor at the Milken Institute School of Public Health of George Washington University, documented in his book Doubt Is Their Product. But the artificial stone slabs that fabrication workers cut to make countertops can contain up to 90% silica, meaning the Osha rule alone is not protective enough, said Michaels, who previously served as assistant secretary of labor for Osha from 2009 to 2017. “It’s also often that many small employers are not in compliance.

events.title: 'Black Swan' investor Mark Spitznagel says you should guard against disaster — but take risks too
events.summary: Mark Spitznagel is the head of Universa Investments. Bloomberg/Getty Images A "Black Swan" investor says to protect yourself against catastrophes while also taking risks. Universa's Mark Spitznagel said it's vital to "bet your beliefs" while avoiding big losses. He told BI that AI won't replace some human skills, and spoke fondly about his best investment. A "Black Swan" investor says to guard against disasters — but take risks too. Mark Spitznagel has built his career on protecting his clients' portfolios against extreme, rare, and unpredictable events known as "black swans" or "tail risks." Yet the Universa Investments founder and chief told Business Insider over coffee in London this month that simply preparing for the worst isn't a winning strategy in life. Not taking enough risks can be the "biggest mistake someone makes," Spitznagel said. "You need to be exposed, you need to bet your beliefs." His career advice mirrors what he says Universa offers to clients : a tail hedge that not only stops them from blowing up, but allows them to be more bullish in their bets. Spitznagel also warned against obsessing over the power of compounding money over time. In his 20s, Warren Buffett famously felt like he was paying $300,000 for a haircut. The legendary investor firmly believed that's how much he could make over time if he invested the money instead of handing it to his barber. Spitznagel said that mindset can be a "curse" because people have to live their lives: "What's the point of compounding if you're not around to see it?" Stay in the game The veteran trader, who ran a hedge fund with "The Black Swan" author Nassim Taleb before starting Universa in 2007, recommended people focus on "mitigating the big losses , not the little ones." "It's not just that it kills you, but it goes down so much, it takes forever to crawl out," he said. He gave the example of an investor taking a 50% loss on a position, then having to make a 100% gain just to break even. Spitznagel championed the " Kelly criterion ," a mathematical formula that can help investors correctly size their bets so they avoid catastrophic losses. He said it's more applicable for people to "think about their life from a Kelly standpoint, rather than just a tail-hedging standpoint." "You can't let your losses take you out of the game," he said. Humans and goats Writing has been one of the most common uses for AI tools like ChatGPT, but Spitznagel said he still expects the " ability to express yourself and write " to remain valuable. The Universa boss said he employs " some of the brightest mathematicians and programmers" on the planet, and they're on the "bleeding edge" of using AI tools. But AI will " never replace basic human judgment," he said. "There will always be an important place for that." Asked to name the best investment he's ever made, Spitznagel pointed to his goat farm in Northport, Michigan. He said that running a farm is "better than anything: yachts, planes, sports teams." He emphasized the satisfaction he gets from "making something tangible," and the pride he feels in producing goat milk and cheese. Spitznagel also said that farming grounds him and connects him to his family, and he enjoys adapting to the different seasons and thinking in very long timeframes . "That's the easiest answer in the world," he said. "It's not even close." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 'It's going to hurt': How a surging student-loan payment is reshaping a family's future
events.summary: The Sprague family is determining the sacrifices they need to make to navigate higher student-loan payments. Alyssa Pointer for BI Jodi and Paul Sprague raised their daughters with a guiding principle: understand the value of a dollar. By elementary school, Evelyn and Olivia were learning about mortgages, car insurance, and basic accounting in the carpool lane. Early one June morning, before Evelyn, 17, and Olivia, 19, left for their summer jobs, Jodi sat them down with news that threw the Spragues' carefully managed budget into question. The student-loan payments the family had budgeted for since 2015 were surging from $404 to $1,014 monthly, starting in September. Jodi Sprague and her daughter, Olivia, are both facing looming student-debt burdens. Alyssa Pointer for BI She and Olivia began to cry. Olivia was about to start her sophomore year at Georgia Southern University, and while her parents helped her pay for housing, that likely wouldn't be possible in the upcoming semester. Her first thought when she learned of Jodi's payment increase: how would she afford her rent? The 150% increase comes from President Donald Trump's student-loan repayment overhaul , which took effect on July 1. It eliminated the Biden-era SAVE repayment plan , which gave Jodi and millions of other borrowers affordable monthly payments. The administration said its changes are intended to curb excessive borrowing, simplify a complex repayment system, and compel colleges to lower their tuition. Over the past year, more than a thousand borrowers have told Business Insider that they're taking on extra work, postponing retirement, and worrying they'll default because of higher monthly bills. This story is part of Business Insider's "Student Debt Spiral" series, which explores how rising student debt is changing the financial futures of millions. Do you have a story to share? Fill out this form , and we'll be in touch. Read more of our student-loan coverage here: 'A bunch of red tape': Student-loan borrowers can't get clear answers from the companies that manage their debt Student-loan borrowers are pushing off retirement , delaying children, and taking on 3 jobs to prep for repayment changes New student-loan repayment glitches are throwing borrowers' budgets into limbo The payment is in Jodi's name, but it will reshape decisions across the household. As Olivia prepares to borrow more for college and Evelyn weighs an expensive career path, Jodi and Paul have to decide how much more work, debt, and sacrifice the family can absorb. "When the kids were little, and there was a dollar in our checking account until payday, we made it," said Jodi, 54. Her student loans are no different. "It's going to hurt," she said, "but I'm going to pay them." Jodi's parents saw college as the key to wealth and pushed their daughters to attend. At 18, she borrowed a minimal amount to pursue a two-year degree at a small Bible college. Looking back, Jodi's shocked it was that easy to take on debt. After seven years as a stay-at-home mom left her depressed and unfulfilled, Jodi decided to go back to school. Teaching would offer the challenge she needed and the career she wanted. Paul, a city employee, worried about managing the cost of a degree while raising a family, but he had faith in Jodi. "She's always been very driven. Very smart." Jodi now has a $144,000 student-loan balance, from a history degree at Kennesaw State University and a master's in teaching from the University of West Georgia. Jodi said she is worried about making her student-loan payment before her next paycheck comes. Alyssa Pointer for BI "We took the maximum out," Jodi, now a middle school teacher, said. "We were able to survive because of the student-loan money." Survival has shaped the Spragues. Two years ago, a tree split open the roof of their home. For a whole school year, the family of four lived in a small rental with their dog Bailey, while their home underwent repairs. "It was absolutely devastating for our family to be literally displaced," Jodi said. "But again, we learned so much from it. We learned that we don't need that much." The first moment Evelyn and Olivia knew they weren't rich was when everyone at kindergarten had American Girl Dolls, but they didn't. They asked for Christmas presents in July to give their parents more time to save up; one year, Olivia got a bottle of Chick-fil-A Polynesian sauce while her friends were getting iPads and cash. When Evelyn's friends wanted to go out to dinner, she was often the one to say no — she had to wait for her next paycheck from Whataburger. In 2011, when the daughters were toddlers, Jodi accumulated credit card debt she couldn't repay, and the Spragues filed for bankruptcy . One day, she didn't know how she'd afford groceries — until an $80 refund check from a dentist appointment arrived in the mail. "I just broke down," Jodi said. "That's how tight it was." We've always had an open dialogue about money because my parents were the opposite. Evelyn and Olivia were too young to understand what bankruptcy meant. Jodi and Paul made it their mission to do what their parents hadn't. "We've always had an open dialogue about money because my parents were the opposite," Jodi said. "They didn't teach us anything. Everything was secret, secret." Jodi and Olivia show their matching tattoos (Evelyn is too young, but she has plans for ink the minute she turns 18). "I remember being in the car line in the morning, and my mom was like, 'You have to get good grades so you can go to school for free,'" Olivia said. "So it's always been in the back of my mind that school is really expensive." events.title: London Underground workers exposed to asbestos without protective masks, documents reveal
events.summary: Hundreds of staff may have worked without legally required face-fitted masks over 20 years Hundreds of London Underground workers could have been exposed to asbestos for almost 20 years without protection required under safety regulations, according to documents seen by the Guardian. Under 2002 rules on controlling asbestos and other hazardous materials, employers are required to take a series of precautions, including ensuring exposed workers are given individually fitted face masks to prevent inhalation of toxic dust. Emails and minutes of meetings reveal that London Underground managers admitted that face-fitted masks were not issued to staff until as late as 2020. The documents suggest Transport for London (TfL), the public body responsible for London Underground, is at risk of more expensive legal claims after already paying out more than £7m in asbestos-related compensation and legal fees. The documents were disclosed as part of an employment tribunal hearing brought by a former London Underground cleaner, Micky Steeds, who successfully claimed he was unfairly dismissed after raising concerns about exposure to asbestos and other toxic dust. In one set of minutes, a manager said he had no recollection or record of face-fitted masks being issued in 2018 to the team responsible for cleaning dust from vents, which included asbestos-sheathed cables. He said such masks were not introduced to London Underground’s civils teams, responsible for all the tube buildings, until late 2020. In December 2020, another manager who was head of lifts and escalators said: “A lot of people aren’t face-fitted,” adding: “Staff shouldn’t have worked without face fit, but it has happened.” He blamed the failure on a lack of training. In 2019, an email from a third manager said allowing Steeds to carry on working without a face-fitted mask was oversight that would be rectified in future. In a 2023 email, a fourth manager admitted that asbestos dust fibre sampling, which is also required under the law, was not conducted. TfL has recorded more than 20,000 asbestos-containing materials across its network, according to data released under freedom of information to Confront Power – an investigative newsletter on industrial harms. TfL insists it has controls in place to manage the risk of asbestos exposure to its staff and the public. In an email in December 2022, a senior engineer responsible for hazardous materials said test results showed levels were “below the relevant workplace exposure limits for both respirable and inhalable dust”. But he said dust being cleaned contained “traces of asbestos fibre occasionally”. But Steeds and one of his former colleagues point out that tests were not conducted while the asbestos was being cleaned and disturbed. And minutes of meetings between staff and a manager also revealed issues with damaged asbestos, which is more dangerous. One experienced cleaner said he encountered asbestos on cables 90% of the time and sometimes: “Broken chunks of asbestos or cable shearing.” Asked what he did when he found asbestos, he said: “We would just carry on and use common sense … don’t bash cables and do what you can.” Catriona Ratcliffe, a solicitor from the personal injury team at LeighDay, said: “Where the asbestos materials are damaged or in poor condition, the risk of exposure is higher because there is more opportunity for the fibres to be released into the atmosphere.” Earlier this year Ratcliffe secured a six-figure settlement from TfL for a former inspector who was diagnosed with sarcomatoid mesothelioma 27 years after supervising the removal of asbestos from the Northern Line. She said the documents in Steeds’ case could result in more injury claims. She added: “If someone is exposed to asbestos over many years, even at low levels, that is going to put that person at risk. And if the employer had knowledge of the risk of exposure, that could result in a legal claim if they have not taken the precautions required under regulations. “Under the control of asbestos regulations [if exposure to asbestos is unavoidable] employers should be giving workers full protection including face-fitted respiratory masks to reduce that risk as far as possible.” Steeds, who was not fitted with a proper mask for 15 months, said: “Over the years, TfL must have put the health of hundreds of workers at risk by failing in their legal duty to provide fitted masks. It makes me so angry that even when I told them about it, they ignored my concerns and tried to cover it up. The incompetent managers who allowed this to happen now have serious questions to answer.” Rob Donnan, a former LU cleaner who is appealing against an employment tribunal’s rejection of his claim for unfair dismissal , said he worked without a fitted mask for three years.

events.title: ‘We can see into the other room’: insurers face surge in subsidence claims
events.summary: Stressed UK homeowners tell of cracks opening up in the walls around them after two record-hot summers “W e’ve got one wall with an absolutely huge diagonal crack, through which we can see through to the other room; you could easily put your fingers in it and chunks of plaster are falling off,” says Henry Biggs, 49, from Stroud in Gloucestershire . He and his partner started noticing cracks in their family home in June 2025, a few months after buying it, and filed an insurance claim for subsidence that was accepted by their insurer, Admiral, in the spring. Monitoring devices were only recently fitted, about a year after they first submitted the claim, and they have no idea when the damage might start to be repaired. They are among a growing number of UK homeowners who face subsidence after two record-hot summers . August was the joint-hottest month ever recorded around the world. Signs of subsidence include widening and lengthening diagonal cracks, typically around window and door frames, as well as sloping floors, and sticking doors and windows. Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, the British Geological Survey has warned. Under its worst-case scenario, 11% of UK homes could be at risk of subsidence by 2070, more than 4.2 million houses. As hotter, drier summers and warmer, wetter winters become more frequent, the ground under houses can shrink and drag down a property’s foundations. Older properties with shallow foundations are more at risk, and those built on clay-rich soils. The most vulnerable areas include London, Essex, Kent and a tranche of land from Oxford up to the Wash on England’s east coast, according to scientists. Insurers have experienced a rise in claims for subsidence in recent months. Hastings says it had record subsidence claims in August , up 140% on last August. So far in 2026, its claims are up by 30% year on year. Axa, one of the biggest home insurers, has talked of a “surge year” for subsidence, and Aviva is reviewing its reserves and pricing models. During this year’s heatwaves the damage at Biggs’s house, which was built in 1970, worsened progressively. “There are cracks now throughout the house, diagonal cracks around almost every window, windows are getting harder to open and close, and the door lintels have dropped, so we have doors now that won’t close,” he says. “In the main part of the house, the kitchen, dining room, the hallway, the floor is dropping and cracking because it’s just falling away in the middle.” He adds: “It’s quite upsetting when you’ve just bought your first home, and we can’t even decorate at the moment.” The couple have hired their own loss assessor as subsidence claims tend to be complex and lengthy, often lasting several years. The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a record £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year. Timothy Farewell, a geospatial environmental data scientist, whose company MapleSky advises 20 insurers, as well as water companies, on ground movement, says: “We have seen widespread drying of soils across the UK in 2018, 2022, 2025 and 2026 leading to an uptick in the number of cracking houses, bursting water mains and failing roads.” It is all about “differential movement”, he says. “You can imagine if your house, road or pipe is built across two different soil types, with one soil more shrinkable than the other, then this differential movement is when you get significant problems, with one part moving more than the other. And differential movement could also happen when you have a tree on one side of the house that is drying out (and shrinking) the soil more on one side of the house than the other.” As old water pipes are more vulnerable than houses to ground movement, summer failures on the water network can indicate that the subsidence risk is increasing in that region. While fewer houses are built on peat-rich soils, movement in these soils has a considerable impact on rural roads and pipe networks, Farewell adds. Shaune Worrall, the deputy head of insurance of the British Insurance Brokers’ Association, has warned of a “double surge” of claims, as many subsidence claims from last year are still being processed. As well as environmental conditions, modern housing layouts can affect the risk, he says. Open-plan extensions, larger kitchens and interconnected living areas can mean that extensive structural repairs are needed. Subsidence excess is usually much higher than for other perils, and a figure of more than £1,000 has become common. This sum could rise to £10,000 for a property that has had subsidence in the past, despite underpinning works. Melissa, who works in the arts and has two children, says she and her husband “reluctantly” lodged an insurance claim for subsidence last month.

events.title: A developer emailed Claude Code's creator about AI slop. Boris Cherny wrote back.
events.summary: Boris Cherny shared his response to a developer worried about AI slop. Bloomberg/Getty Images A developer emailed Claude Code creator Boris Cherny that AI coding had created "friction." Cherny posted his full response to the engineer. The developer's job is to "hold the bar on code quality," Cherny wrote. Developers are worried about AI. The creator of Claude Code has a response. On Thursday, Anthropic's Boris Cherny posted an email a developer wrote to him on X. The email was titled: "What to do about slop?" Cherny wrote that he receives emails like this every day and that he tries to respond to as many as possible. It's no surprise that developers are reaching out to Cherny with their worries. AI has radically changed coding , shifting job descriptions and turning engineers into reviewers. Some engineers love the ease; others call it lonely and tedious . In the email, the unnamed developer wrote that the shift to AI coding was causing "friction." He broke it down into two views and asked Cherny to broker the dispute. The first view was a more restrained use of AI tools: We create code similar to before, accelerated by AI. We may not review all of it, but it should be reviewable. The person submitting the code should be able to explain it. It should be built in such a way to make it as easy to maintain — or easier — than before, by human agents. The second view was more permissive. This was the vibe coding position: We treat the code as a black box. We don't worry about it. We just check the output. The developer wrote that many people were incapable of doing option 1 — the more restrained approach — but worried about getting laid off . "A lot of people are just forcing it," they wrote. Cherny posted his response in full. As for the two options the developer provided, Cherny said there was room for both. On the "don't worry" approach: Prototypes and other throw-away code can be treated as totally black box. If you're going to throw it away anyway, and if the blast radius of it breaking is low, it doesn't need to be perfect. And, on cautious reviewing: Production code written by Claude should have a higher bar than if it was written by a human. At Anthropic, we have many guardrails in place to make sure this is happening: lots of lint rules, lots of tests, Claude-driven end to end tests, Claude-powered fuzzers running daily, automated code reviews and security reviews, automated code refactoring, and so on. Without these, you can end up with a mess that is hard to maintain down the line. Luckily, the model makes it increasingly easy to do these well — run a few daily routines, use Claude Code Review, etc. The developer's job is to "hold the bar on code quality," Cherny wrote. AI leaders use different terms for this role, such as " mini CEO ." It's the developer's job to act like a manager, stopping bad code in its tracks. If all else fails, Cherny said the developer could be more hands-on with Claude or ask it to rewrite the codebase. "Or, wait for the next model," he wrote. events.title: Miss USA contestants sold vacation packages and asked fans to buy votes. It's the CEO's latest effort to stay relevant.
events.summary: Contestants at the 2026 Miss USA pageant in Miami on August 27. Ivan Apfel/Getty Images The 2,400-seat Miami theater lit up like a Coldplay concert when the QR code dropped at the Miss USA pageant . A sea of phones — held up by supportive parents, partners, and past pageant queens — trained their cameras on the massive barcode being projected from center stage, ready to vote for their favored contestant. Twelve minutes on the clock: The countdown was on. Fingers tapped rapidly as the audience used their free vote or purchased more in bundles — $50 for 50, $250 for 250, $500 for 500 — alongside viewers at home. The top 20 contestants' headshots shifted around the leaderboard as the votes tallied live on the pageant's website, revealing exactly how far each woman was from the top spot. Two minutes left on the clock, a banner flashed across: Now, votes counted double. As the seconds ticked closer to zero, the votes burst in like a flash flood. The gap between first and second place was 1,794 votes at the 36-second mark. When the clock struck zero, it was more than 14,000. Fans have never had more of a say at Miss USA — especially if they're willing to pay. At last month's pageant, paid voting helped determine three top 20 spots, while a fourth went to the contestant who sold the most Westgate Resorts vacation packages, an unprecedented incentive that tied a contestant's placement to sales for a pageant sponsor. The winner was determined by a panel of six judges, including a mix of Miss USA and Miss Universe winners , but fans also had the opportunity to vote for the top 10 as the "seventh judge." Nearly a dozen of this year's Miss USA contestants spoke to Business Insider about the changes. Some believe it's a savvy strategy by CEO Thom Brodeur , who took over the pageant in September 2025, to keep the business afloat and increase fan engagement, especially at a time when pageants struggle to remain relevant. Others worry the competition is turning into what one called a "pay-to-play" model, making it less accessible to women who don't have money or big social media followings. Nobody is arguing with Beyoncé or Taylor Swift's teams over the standing-room ticket prices of four-figures and higher, and we're not going to apologize either. Miss USA CEO Thom Brodeur "There's a lot of fatigue," Miss Arizona Kaitlyn Humphrey told Business Insider. "It's an expensive sport already, and it breaks my heart that a lot of people can't compete purely because there's such a barrier to entry in the financial aspect of things. And then we're just adding layers to that." The bygone days of network TV Bob Barker hosted the Miss USA 1972 pageant, which aired on CBS. Bettmann/Bettmann Archive Nearly 40 million people tuned in to watch Miss USA in the 1960s and '70s, but viewership dwindled over its 60 years on television. In 2023, the Miss USA final peaked at 1.1 million viewers on The CW. It was a far cry from its heyday, but still enough for a multiyear deal. The network ultimately dropped the pageant in 2025 amid fallout from former CEO Laylah Rose 's tenure, during which Miss USA 2023 Noelia Voigt and Miss Teen USA 2023 UmaSofia Srivastava relinquished their crowns due to her leadership. This year, the competition was set to return to The CW, but, as Business Insider first reported, the network dropped the show on August 20, a week before the final. Miss USA cited a "contractual issue with our production arrangements" and moved it to Queen Beauty Network, a streaming service focused on the pageant industry, where Brodeur is listed as vice president and chief marketing officer. When the crown was placed on Justus Kelley's head on August 27, making her the first married woman and mother to win the title , a live viewer counter on the Queen Beauty Network showed around 4,000 people watching. Shrinking viewership hasn't only affected Miss USA's ratings — it's put a serious dent in the pageant's coffers. Paula Shugart, who oversaw Miss USA from 2001 to 2020 as president of the Miss Universe Organization, told Business Insider that the pageant once received $3 to $5 million in licensing fees from the networks. Those days are gone. "Sharknado" star Ian Ziering and Miss USA 1993 Kenya Moore hosted the 2026 Miss USA finals. Ivan Apfel/Getty Images "Network television has completely changed," Shugart said. "You don't have the viewership, and you're not going to get the license fees that you used to get. You have to figure out different ways to pay for it and defray the costs." It's a reality that Brodeur knows well. "The days of 'free lunch' for pageants and pageant fans are over," he told Business Insider last week. "They've been over for some time. Introducing new revenue streams — whether that's through fan voting, contests, or other unique opportunities we're exploring — are the way this industry lives to see its next 75 years." Competing at Miss USA wasn't cheap to begin with, although the cost varies widely depending on who you ask. Contestants who spoke to Business Insider estimated costs ranging from $3,000 to $50,000. Brodeur compared the investment to that of any competitive sport. "There is nothing new under the sun about creating opportunities and spaces for all of us to exercise our God-given gifts in this world," he said. "Unfortunately, there are also costs attached to the creation of those opportunities and spaces, and that's the reality of life." A new way to engage fans Justus Kelley, who won Miss USA 2026, with Miss Florida Aileen Cerchiara and Miss Pennsylvania Elizabeth Voight during the finals. Ivan Apfel/Getty Images Traditionally, contestants make it to Miss USA by winning a state pageant. Those are organized and funded by individual directors, who pay the organization a franchise fee. Contestants must live, work, or study in the state for at least 90 days prior to the competition and are allowed to compete in two state pageants a year. When Brodeur took over as CEO , he had five weeks to put on the Miss USA 2025 pageant . Some departed state directors had not been replaced, and eight states were missing titleholders. His solution: an open casting call in which women from any state could apply for a state title. Five judges selected the titleholders. This year, 16 states were left without directors. Brodeur said only the Miss Universe Organization can legally issue franchise agreements to new state directors, so the open casting call returned — this time with fans getting a say. Before the applicants could be seen by a judging panel of former Miss USA winners , they had to make it through three rounds of fan voting over the course of a month. People could use a daily free vote or purchase bundles that ranged from $4.99 for 10 votes to $499 for 2,000 votes on a third-party website. events.title: Meet the NYC parents who feel like their toddlers got into Harvard
events.summary: A new 2-K student poses for her first day in the program. Paola Chapdelaine for BI When Zaire Wells's daughter was selected for a free childcare slot, it felt like the two-year-old "got into Harvard." NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani proposed free childcare for two-year-olds in his affordability-focused campaign. In March, he announced that it would launch with 2,000 seats in a handful of communities selected for economic need and childcare demand . Wells, a high school teacher, lives in one of the targeted areas. After a five-minute online application back in June, she and her partner were now tearfully dropping off their daughter for her first day at a Friends of Crown Heights center in Brooklyn. The family posed for pictures with a staged first-day backdrop, the two-year-old curiously examining her new surroundings. Wells' Harvard comparison was apt: Lisa Joseph-Mayers, who works with families in the center, said the program received 339 applications for 12 slots. That's a 3.5% acceptance rate; Harvard accepted 4.2% for the class of 2029. At least two parents called during school drop-off to see if they could snag a seat, and were told that the program was full. "It's going to be like that for the rest of the week," Joseph-Mayers said. Since students with siblings already in the center were given preference, Joseph-Mayers said, some families claimed distant family connections to try to finagle a spot. Business Insider wants to hear from parents with kids in 2-K, or care centers offering the program. Contact this reporter at jkaplan@businessinsider.com if you have a story to share. The city has said that more than 5,700 applications were submitted for around 2,000 available seats. The popularity of the new program has become a double-edged sword, as some centers were reportedly left without the necessary funding to open, and others scrambled to determine whether they could secure bridge loans in time for the first day. For a program intended to expand sixfold by next year, it highlights a set of growing pains that are currently falling on providers. When asked about the funding delays, the city cited previous remarks by the mayor and Gov. Kathy Hochul. Lisa Joseph-Mayers fielded calls from parents hoping to get their kids into the program. Paola Chapdelaine for BI "I think it's critically important that we both address longstanding issues in our New York City public school system and advance an agenda that makes it more affordable for families to stay in this city," Mamdani said at a September 10 press conference. Friends of Crown Heights hasn't encountered those issues, according to Tanya McDougal, the site's educational director; they'd previously had a two-year-old classroom, and reopening it was relatively seamless. The two-year-olds were hard at work just 15 minutes into the day. Paola Chapdelaine for BI Jessica Arroyo, who was dropping off her daughter, said it meant "everything" to be accepted into the program. The program's hours, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., were particularly appealing to Arroyo, who works in registration at a hospital. "I can work in peace," Arroyo said. "She can learn, make new friends." For Mercy and Fabian Best, who were dropping off their daughter — complete with a photo sign indicating it was her first day — the slot offered financial relief . The money they're saving on their two-year-old's care — on average, infant and toddler care costs in the city can top $20,000 annually — means they can put more toward their older child's extracurriculars at public school. The center before the back-to-school rush. Paola Chapdelaine for BI "New York City is very expensive, and one less thing you have to worry about — while receiving quality education — helps us in the long run," Fabian said. The two-year-olds hadn't received the message that they were part of New York City childcare history : Parents tried to wrangle their children for a photo — there were a lot of "big emotions" among the students, including crying, sleepiness, and the desire to start dancing. Within fifteen or so minutes, though, the two-year-olds had gotten to work in their classroom. One was using a toy broom to sweep up the room, another was organizing the play kitchen, and — like good New Yorkers — several were yelling "pizza!" as they played with fake plastic slices. There was also a brief toy car traffic jam, as well as some serious xylophone playing. When I asked Journey, Arroyo's daughter, what she wanted to do that day, her answer was simple: "Move." That wish came true when Ms. Lisa later played her some toddler tunes; Journey busted out a whole little dance, happy to jam with her new friends. Read the original article on Business Insider
